title: Francis Bacon: Study from the Human Body Poster
description:
This oversize poster reproduces Study from the Human Body (1986), one of three late paintings by Francis Bacon shown in the exhibition Francis Bacon at Gagosian's rue de Castiglione gallery in Paris.

The exhibition, on view April 11-May 30, 2026, brought together three major canvases from Bacon's final period and reaffirmed his ties to Paris, where he kept a studio from 1975 to 1987. In the painting, a solitary, contorted figure crouches against a sharp yellow ground while a red arrow points toward its confinement; the yellow recalls a group of paintings Bacon made in 1969, among them a triptych of Lucian Freud.

Bacon (1909-1992) spent his career returning to the human figure, painting distorted bodies and faces charged with psychological intensity. This poster, produced in 2026, carries the imagery of one of his last major statements on that subject.

title: Sarah Sze: Feel Free Poster
description:
This poster reproduces a detail from Feel Free (2026), a large-format painting Sarah Sze made for her exhibition Sarah Sze: Feel Free at Gagosian, Beverly Hills.

The exhibition, held January 29-February 28, 2026, paired two immersive video installations with a new series of large-format paintings built from Sze's ongoing redefinition of collage as a spatial and temporal language. The paintings layer glimpses of observed and remembered scenes, produced through repeated fragmentation and reconstruction, into compositions of shifting scale and tempo.

Sze (b. 1969) works across sculpture, painting, drawing, video, and installation, assembling physical and digital fragments into environments that move between the microscopic and the macroscopic. Her paintings extend that practice onto a two-dimensional surface, tracking how memory and perception form under constant media exposure.

title: Richard Prince: Canal Zone Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Graduation (2008), a work from Richard Prince's Canal Zone series, produced in 2014 for Richard Prince: Canal Zone at Gagosian's Madison Avenue gallery in New York (May 8–June 14, 2014).

The Canal Zone paintings combine paint with photographs appropriated from other photographers' work, most notably Patrick Cariou's images of Rastafarians in Jamaica. The series became the subject of the copyright case Cariou v. Prince, which tested the legal limits of appropriation art. Graduation shows Prince's layering of collaged photographic fragments with loosely painted additions.

Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) has worked since the late 1970s by rephotographing and recontextualizing images from advertising, pulp fiction, and mass media, questioning the conventions of authorship and originality. Canal Zone remains one of the more contested chapters in that project, and its Gagosian exhibition placed the series within the gallery's long representation of his work.

title: Sarah Sze: Rip Tide Poster
description:
Sarah Sze made Rip Tide (2025) for Sarah Sze, the exhibition that marked her first show in Asia, at Gagosian, Hong Kong; this poster reproduces a detail from the painting.

The exhibition, on view March 25-May 3, 2025, included new mixed-media paintings alongside a series of hanging sculptures. In Rip Tide, a collaged image of a bird soars over a sweep of pink, orange, and gold paint that echoes a flock of birds rising toward the top of the canvas, part of Sze's recurring interest in motion caught mid-transformation.

Sze (b. 1969) builds paintings, sculptures, and installations from layered images and objects, working between memory and material. In works like this one, recurring imagery surfaces and dissolves across the canvas the way details resurface and fade in memory. This record covers the unsigned poster; Gagosian also sold a version signed by the artist.

title: Picasso and Marie-Thérèse: L'amour fou Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Pablo Picasso's Deux femmes enlacées (1936) and was produced in 2011 for the exhibition Picasso and Marie-Thérèse: L'amour fou at Gagosian's West 21st Street gallery in New York.

The exhibition was curated by Picasso biographer John Richardson and by art historian Diana Widmaier-Picasso, Marie-Thérèse Walter's granddaughter. It brought together more than eighty paintings, drawings, sculptures, and prints made between 1927 and 1940, tracing Picasso's decade of work inspired by Walter, one of his most important models. The painting reproduced here shows two entwined female figures, a composition tied to the artist's Le Sauvetage series, which depicted Walter's near drowning and rescue.

Picasso (1881–1973) painted Walter obsessively between the late 1920s and 1940, moving between tender portraiture and forms bent toward abstraction. The Gagosian exhibition placed this canvas within that sustained body of work rather than presenting it as an isolated image.

The exhibition included over 80 works spanning 1927–1940. Only one (unsigned) variant of this poster was offered; sold unframed.

title: Richard Prince: High Times Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Untitled (2017), a painting from Richard Prince's High Times series, made in 2018 for Richard Prince: High Times at Gagosian's West 21st Street gallery in New York (November 1–December 15, 2018).

The High Times paintings combine oil stick, acrylic, charcoal, collage, and inkjet on canvas, building crowded fields of invented cartoon-like figures. Reviewing the exhibition for the New York Times, Roberta Smith described the series as a web of cross-references reflecting Prince's habit of mixing fact and fiction across his interests in rock music, collecting, and postwar literature. Untitled (2017) measures 96 × 72 1/2 inches and shares that dense, layered surface.

Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) has worked since the late 1970s by appropriating and reworking images and personas drawn from American subcultures and mass media. High Times pushed that practice toward invented figuration, building crowded, cartoonish compositions rather than reworking a single found image.

title: Richard Prince: Early Photography, 1977–87 Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Untitled (Sunset) (1982), a photograph from Richard Prince's early appropriation work, made in 2023 for Richard Prince: Early Photography, 1977–87 at Gagosian, Grosvenor Hill, London (October 5–December 22, 2023).

The exhibition surveyed the cowboy, girlfriend, and advertisement photographs Prince made by rephotographing images from magazines and advertising, a method he adopted in 1977 that recast questions of authorship and originality. Untitled (Sunset) shows a boy holding a clown puppet, rendered in low-resolution black and white against a red-orange ground that suggests the end of day.

Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) built his early reputation on this rephotography method, extracting images from their original commercial context and re-presenting them as his own. The 1977–87 photographs remain the foundation for the appropriation strategies he later carried into painting and collage.

title: Richard Prince: Hoods Poster
description:
This poster reproduces a 1987 photograph of Richard Prince in his Reade Street studio in New York, with several early works from his Hoods series, made in 2022 for Richard Prince: Hoods at Gagosian, 522 West 21st Street, New York (May 10–June 25, 2022).

The exhibition was the first to bring together this body of paintings, made using the hoods of muscle cars as supports. The poster is printed in Daytona Orange, a color long associated with muscle cars and motorcycles, tying its production to the material the paintings are built from. The studio photograph is credited to Joseph Coscia Jr.

Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) began the Hoods series in the 1980s, treating automotive parts as both surface and subject within his broader engagement with American car culture. The 1987 studio photograph documents the series near its origin, decades before the Gagosian exhibition brought it to wider view.

title: Cy Twombly: A Survey of Photographs, 1954–2011 Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Brushes, Lexington (2008/2009), a photograph by Cy Twombly made for his 2012 exhibition Cy Twombly: A Survey of Photographs, 1954–2011.

Gagosian staged the show at once in Beverly Hills, London, and New York. It was the first major survey of Twombly's photographs shown in either the United States or the United Kingdom, tracing nearly six decades of the practice from early black-and-white studies to the large color prints of his last years. Brushes, Lexington is a close, soft-focus view of paintbrushes standing in a jar in the artist's studio, the kind of blurred, intimate image he made repeatedly of his own working spaces.

Twombly (1928–2011) took up photography in the early 1950s. He kept at it throughout his career, a private practice alongside his painting and sculpture that he began enlarging on a color copier in the 1990s. The 2012 survey was the first exhibition to present that body of photographs on the same scale as his work in other mediums.
tags: Art, Posters, Exhibition Poster, Ephemera, Photography, Studio Photography
notes: Poster reproduces Brushes, Lexington (2008/2009), a photograph, not a painting; produced 2012 for the exhibition A Survey of Photographs, 1954–2011, staged concurrently at Gagosian Beverly Hills (April 27–June 9, 2012), London (September 6–29, 2012), and New York (November 1–December 22, 2012) — the first major exhibition of Twombly's photographs in the US and UK.

title: Titus Kaphar: Analogous Colors Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Analogous Colors (2020), a painting by Titus Kaphar made for the cover of Time magazine's June 15, 2020 issue, accompanied by the artist's own text, "I cannot sell you this painting."

Gagosian produced the poster in 2021 for Titus Kaphar: From a Tropical Space, an exhibition at the gallery's West 21st Street space in New York. The painting depicts a Black mother holding her child, whose form is left an empty white silhouette; Kaphar made the work and its accompanying text in the days after George Floyd's killing by Minneapolis police, addressing the vulnerability of Black families to violence and loss.

Kaphar works across painting, sculpture, and film, often cutting, folding, or erasing sections of his own canvases to question how Western art history has depicted Black subjects. The empty silhouette in Analogous Colors is one instance of that method, applied here to the aftermath of a killing rather than to a historical painting.

title: Anna Weyant: The Guitar Man Poster
description:
This poster reproduces The Return of The Girls Next Door (2022–23), a painting by Anna Weyant made for her exhibition Anna Weyant: The Guitar Man.

Gagosian produced the poster in 2023 for the show's run at the gallery's rue de Castiglione space in Paris, Weyant's European solo debut. Titled after a song by the Los Angeles band Bread, the exhibition paired new figure paintings with still lifes referencing American pop culture, from The Addams Family to Playboy, and continued the dollhouse motif from her earlier work. The Return of The Girls Next Door shows three women from behind, painted in the deep chiaroscuro that runs through the series.

Weyant, born in Calgary in 1995 and trained at the Rhode Island School of Design, paints young women in scenes of low-stakes trauma set against a muted, tonal palette drawn from seventeenth-century Dutch painting. The Guitar Man was among the exhibitions that led to her first solo institutional show, at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid in 2025.

title: Cy Twombly: In Beauty it is finished Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Untitled (2001), a work on paper by Cy Twombly made for the 2018 exhibition Cy Twombly: In Beauty it is finished, Drawings 1951–2008.

Held at Gagosian's West 21st Street gallery in New York, the show was the first career-spanning survey of Twombly's drawings and works on paper, timed to the completion of the Cy Twombly: Catalogue Raisonné of Drawings, edited by Nicola Del Roscio. Untitled, in acrylic, wax crayon, and cut-and-pasted paper, belongs to the artist's late paper works, built up in loops, smears, and drips that pay little attention to which way is down.

Twombly (1928–2011) drew throughout his six-decade career, using paper as a ground for gesture, script, and erasure with the same seriousness he brought to canvas. The 2018 exhibition and the catalogue raisonné it accompanied argued for drawing as a continuous line through his work rather than a study for the paintings.
tags: Art, Posters, Exhibition Poster, Ephemera, Works on Paper, Drawing
notes: Poster reproduces Untitled (2001), a work on paper (acrylic, wax crayon, and cut-and-pasted paper on paper, per the poster's own caption; Gagosian's product copy says 'oil stick and wax crayon' — the caption is preferred here), not a painting; produced 2018 for In Beauty it is finished, Drawings 1951–2008, at Gagosian, West 21st Street, New York, March 8–April 25, 2018, which coincided with the completion of the Cy Twombly: Catalogue Raisonné of Drawings, edited by Nicola Del Roscio.

title: Jeff Wall: Mother of pearl Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Jeff Wall's photograph Mother of pearl (2016) and was produced in 2019 for Jeff Wall, his first exhibition with Gagosian, at the gallery's West 21st Street location in New York.

The photograph shows a child in a room furnished with antique furniture and keepsakes, absorbed in a set of iridescent mother-of-pearl game counters spread across an open box. Wall builds the image from an ordinary domestic setting, using it to stage a child's private absorption within a heavily decorated adult interior.

Wall (b. 1946, Vancouver) has worked since the late 1970s in large-scale color photography, moving between elaborately staged tableaux and scenes closer to documentary observation. Mother of pearl belongs to the constructed side of that practice, and this 2019 exhibition marked the start of his representation by Gagosian.

title: Cy Twombly: Lepanto Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Naumachia (1992), a tempera and pencil work on paper by Cy Twombly, made in 2002 for the exhibition Cy Twombly: Lepanto at Gagosian's 555 West 24th Street gallery in New York.

The exhibition presented Lepanto, a painting in twelve parts first shown at the 49th Biennale di Venezia in the summer of 2001, which depicts the sixteenth-century naval battle in which the combined European fleet under Venetian command defeated the Ottoman navy. Naumachia is a related work on paper rather than one of the twelve panels, its title borrowed from the staged sea battles once mounted for public entertainment in ancient Rome.

Twombly (1928–2011) returned to classical and military history across his career, from the Fifty Days at Iliam paintings of the 1970s to Lepanto's later treatment of empire and combat. The New York exhibition brought the cycle, painted and first exhibited in Venice the year before, to his primary American gallery.
tags: Art, Posters, Exhibition Poster, Ephemera, Painting, Venice Biennale
notes: Poster reproduces Naumachia (1992, tempera and pencil on paper) — a related work on paper, not one of the twelve panels of the Lepanto cycle itself. The exhibition Cy Twombly: Lepanto, at Gagosian, 555 West 24th Street, New York, January 19–February 26, 2002, showed the twelve-part painting Lepanto, first exhibited at the 49th Biennale di Venezia in summer 2001. Lepanto depicts the 1571 naval battle of Venetian-led European forces against the Ottoman fleet.

title: Richard Prince: Bob Dylan Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Untitled (Dylan) (2014), one of a trio of ten-foot-square paintings Richard Prince made for Richard Prince: Bob Dylan, an exhibition at Gagosian, Beverly Hills, in 2025.

Each painting in the trio renders, in blurred black and white, a detail of Jerry Schatzberg's 1966 portrait of Bob Dylan, the image John Berg used for the cover of the double LP Blonde on Blonde. Schatzberg's photograph was already soft-focus, reportedly because he was shivering in the cold when he shot it; Prince pushes that blur further across the three canvases, each one hazier than the last.

Prince (b. 1949, Panama Canal Zone) has repeatedly returned to photographs already loaded with cultural weight, reworking them to hold both familiarity and distance at once. The Dylan paintings extend that approach to an image inseparable from a specific record and era, treating a fixed piece of pop history as material still open to revision.

title: Cy Twombly: Paesaggio Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Paesaggio (1986), a painting by Cy Twombly shown in the 2025 exhibition Cy Twombly at Gagosian's 980 Madison Avenue gallery in New York.

The painting belongs to a group of green-toned canvases Twombly made at his studio in Bassano in Teverina, Italy, between 1981 and 1986, working from the landscape around him. Thinned, liquid paint builds up in layers so that water, earth, and air read as loosely bound rather than as separate elements, with color and texture carrying the sense of place rather than describing it directly.

Twombly (1928–2011) settled in Italy in the late 1950s and worked between Bassano in Teverina and Gaeta for much of his later career, moving from the classical references of his Roman years toward the more abstract, landscape-based paintings of the 1980s. Paesaggio belongs to that later group.
tags: Art, Posters, Exhibition Poster, Ephemera, Painting, Landscape

title: Pop Art Is. . . (Ed Ruscha) Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Ed Ruscha's Bundle of Pencils, Breaking Glass (1968–69) and was produced in 2007 for Pop Art Is. . ., a group exhibition at Gagosian's Britannia Street gallery in London.

Marking fifty years since Richard Hamilton's definition of Pop art, the exhibition brought together artists addressing how the term's meaning had shifted since. Ruscha's painting sets a bundle of yellow pencils and a glass caught mid-break against a plain ground, rendered in the flat, illustrational style he uses for trompe l'oeil images of ordinary objects.

Ruscha (b. 1937) moved to Los Angeles in 1956 and built a practice around vernacular language and objects rendered with commercial precision. Bundle of Pencils, Breaking Glass reflects his recurring interest in manipulating scale and surface within plain, everyday subjects. The London show placed the painting within a wider survey of Pop's legacy rather than presenting it as part of a Ruscha solo exhibition.

title: Paris Review: Anna Weyant Poster
description:
This poster reproduces the cover of the Spring 2025 issue of The Paris Review, featuring Anna Weyant's painting Night Flowers (2024–25).

The issue, per its own cover line, gathers prose, poetry, interviews, and art. Night Flowers depicts a glass vase of white and yellow blooms rendered flat and cartoonish, painted in the subdued, dark-toned palette Weyant favors, recalling Dutch still-life painters such as Gerrit van Honthorst and Judith Leyster. A crack in the vase leaks water that drips down the ledge beneath it, a small disruption in an otherwise composed arrangement.

Still lifes like this one sit alongside Weyant's figure paintings of young women as a second strand of her work, sharing its muted tonal range and its habit of placing a small wrong note inside a composed scene. The artist has summarized the approach directly: "the sinister can often be masked by beauty."

title: Cy Twombly: Untitled (2007) Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Untitled (2007), a painting by Cy Twombly shown in the 2022 exhibition Cy Twombly at Gagosian, Beverly Hills, a survey spanning paintings, sculptures, and works on paper.

The painting sets cursive lines, sweeping arcs, and drips of red paint against a yellow ground, a gestural language that goes back to the grey and white "blackboard" paintings Twombly made in the 1960s and early 1970s. Here the scale is larger and the palette saturated rather than restrained, part of a return to large-format painting that ran through his final decade.

Twombly (1928–2011) worked across painting, drawing, sculpture, and photography over six decades, dividing his time between Italy and the United States. In his last paintings, Untitled (2007) among them, he revisited the gestures of his earliest abstract work at a scale and color intensity he had not used before.

title: Jenny Saville a Ca' Pesaro Poster
description:
This poster reproduces a detail from Jenny Saville's Focus (2022–24), made for her first major exhibition in Venice, Jenny Saville a Ca' Pesaro.

The exhibition ran at Ca' Pesaro–Galleria Internazionale d'Arte Moderna from March 28 to November 22, 2026, bringing together more than thirty canvases and works on paper spanning the 1990s to the present. It placed Saville's paintings in dialogue with the museum's collection of Venetian masters, tracing the development of her practice and its roots in art history. Focus is a close-cropped portrait head built up in heavy, worked layers of oil paint, in the manner Saville uses across her figure paintings.

Saville (b. 1970, Cambridge) studied at the Glasgow School of Art and emerged with the Young British Artists in the early 1990s, painting the body at monumental scale and drawing on Titian, Tintoretto and de Kooning alongside surgical and medical imagery. The National Portrait Gallery in London gave her a major exhibition in 2025.

title: Seeing Is Believing: Lee Miller and Friends Poster
description:
This poster reproduces Man Ray's Shadow Patterns on Lee Miller's Torso (1930), made for the exhibition Seeing Is Believing: Lee Miller and Friends.

The show ran at Gagosian, 976 Madison Avenue, New York, from November 11 to December 22, 2023. It centered on the long working relationship between the American photographer Lee Miller and the English Surrealist painter and collector Roland Penrose, and included work by artists in their circle: Joseph Cornell, Max Ernst, Dora Maar, Man Ray, Henry Moore, Valentine Penrose and Pablo Picasso. In the photograph, light falling through a curtain casts a grid of shadow across Miller's torso, its lines following the contours of her figure.

Man Ray (1890–1976) and Miller (1907–1977) met in Paris in 1929, when she became his student, model and collaborator; together they developed solarization and other darkroom techniques central to Surrealist photography. Miller later built her own career as a photographer and, during the Second World War, as a correspondent for Vogue. The photograph dates from the height of their partnership in Paris.
